lines.say: Chapter one. No more E.

Enron was formed in nineteen eighty-five, from the merger of two natural gas pipeline companies, and it grew through the nineteen-nineties, largely on energy trading. Before it filed for bankruptcy, the grand jury later wrote, it was the seventh largest corporation in the United States.

lines.say: So, the government said, he set out to convince the market that Enron was poised for steady and significant growth. Two newer businesses carried that story: Enron Energy Services, which sold energy at retail, and Enron Broadband Services, its move into telecommunications.

lines.say: Chapter two. Beat the street.

Wall Street analysts estimate what a company will earn each quarter. The average is called the consensus estimate. Skilling, the appeals court wrote, was particularly committed to hitting or beating it, according to the government.

scene.kicker: AS THE FIFTH CIRCUIT DESCRIBED IT
scene.src: United States v. Skilling, No. 06-20885 (5th Cir., Jan 2009)

lines.say: In mid two thousand, the consensus was thirty-two cents a share. A draft showed Enron would meet it. Skilling wanted thirty-four. He allegedly told the wholesale division to add seven million dollars of earnings, and then seven million more. Fourteen million dollars came out of a reserve account set aside for potential liabilities.
lines.show: In mid-2000, the consensus was 32¢ a share. A draft showed Enron would meet it. Skilling wanted 34¢. He allegedly told the wholesale division to add $7 million of earnings, and then $7 million more. $14 million came out of a reserve account set aside for potential liabilities.

lines.say: Chapter four. The exit.

On August fourteenth, two thousand one, about six months after becoming chief executive, Skilling abruptly resigned. By then, the government said, he knew Enron was suffering substantial undisclosed losses. Kenneth Lay, who had run Enron before him, took the job back.
